## Introduction to Copyright

Copyright represents a collection of exclusive rights held by creators over their original works,
including authority over how their creations are utilised and distributed.

The [Berne Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berne_Convention), an international treaty adopted
by most nations worldwide, establishes fundamental copyright principles and promotes consistency in
intellectual property protection globally. Greece, as a member state of the EU, implements these
principles through national law and EU directives on copyright and related rights.

By default, copyright functions under an "all rights reserved" model, restricting others from accessing,
copying, modifying, or sharing work without explicit authorisation. Licences serve as the mechanism to
grant these permissions.

## Copyright at CERTH

At CERTH, employed personnel — including permanent researchers, engineers, and affiliated staff —
typically have the works produced within the scope of their professional activities held by their
respective CERTH Institute as the copyright owner, in accordance with Greek employment and intellectual
property law.

Before publishing any work that incorporates third-party contributions, securing signed agreements or
valid licences from the relevant copyright holders is essential. This applies equally to code,
documentation, datasets, and design files.

When in doubt about copyright ownership — especially in collaborative or externally funded projects —
consult the CERTH OSPO before proceeding.

## What Copyright Protects

Copyright protects original expression. In the context of research and engineering at CERTH, this
includes:

- **Source code** — programs, scripts, configuration files with sufficient creative content
- **Documentation** — written descriptions, manuals, and tutorials
- **Diagrams and figures** — technical illustrations and design schematics
- **Datasets with creative structure** — curated collections where the selection or arrangement is
  original

Copyright does **not** protect:

- **Ideas or algorithms in the abstract** — only their specific expression
- **Purely factual data** — raw measurements, numerical results without creative arrangement
- **Standard interfaces or formats** — names, signatures, and protocols

Understanding this boundary helps define the scope of the rights you hold and the permissions others
need when using your work.

## Third-Party Components

Many research software projects incorporate libraries, datasets, or code from external sources. Before
open-sourcing, you must:

1. **Identify all third-party components** and their respective copyright holders
2. **Verify the licence** of each component is compatible with your intended project licence
3. **Preserve existing copyright notices** — these must not be removed or altered

See the [Due Diligence](due-diligence.qmd) page for a structured approach to this analysis.
